items.explanation: Obergefell belongs to the long, ongoing story of rights expansion: the review traces the line from the 1960s movements through later decisions and beyond, presenting civil rights as an unfinished continuity rather than a closed chapter.
items.fact_source: u9.md §What the exam tests here — treat civil rights as an unfinished continuity: trace the line from the 1960s movements through Obergefell and beyond

option_explanations.A: Right because the decision continues the post-1960s expansion of civil rights into the present.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because civil rights litigation continued after 2015.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the decision expanded marriage rights, moving away from 1950s norms.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because Obergefell rested on the 14th Amendment's equal protection and due process guarantees.

options: (A) Civil rights as an ongoing story: from the 1960s movements through later expansions into the present
(B) The end of all civil rights litigation in America
(C) A return to 1950s social norms
(D) The Supreme Court's rejection of the 14th Amendment's equal protection guarantee for gay Americans
items.stem: In Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), the Supreme Court established a constitutional right to same-sex marriage nationwide. Which broader development best explains the context of this decision?

stimulus.text: Obergefell v. Hodges (2015): the Supreme Court nationalized same-sex marriage, building on decades of rights litigation.

items.explanation: Bush v. Gore left the country evenly and bitterly divided after a recount halted by the Court. It stands as an early marker of the polarization — institutional distrust, impeachment politics, and unresolved arguments about elections — that deepened through the 2000s and 2010s.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — the 2000 election, decided by the Supreme Court in Bush v. Gore, left the country evenly and bitterly divided; §What the exam tests here — explain polarization: know the markers — the 2000 election, impeachment politics, the Tea Party

option_explanations.A: Wrong because television shaped elections starting in 1960, not 2000.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the election was extraordinarily close, not a landslide.
option_explanations.C: Right because the disputed outcome became a defining marker of the polarized era.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because both sides contested the process; the Court's intervention was itself controversial.

options: (A) It was the first presidential election ever to involve television coverage
(B) It produced a landslide victory that ended partisan division
(C) It left the nation evenly divided, marking the polarization and distrust that deepened after
(D) Both candidates agreed the Supreme Court had no constitutional authority to decide the election
items.stem: The 2000 presidential election was decided by the Supreme Court in Bush v. Gore, which halted the Florida recount. Which broader development best explains why this election is treated as a marker of a new political era?

stimulus.text: Bush v. Gore (2000): the Supreme Court halted the Florida recount, deciding the presidency and leaving the nation evenly and bitterly divided.

items.explanation: The review's verdict is direct: the invasion was launched on WMD claims that proved false, the occupation was long and costly, the country split over it, and the episode discredited the neoconservative vision of remaking the Middle East through American military power after 9/11.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — in 2003 the invasion of Iraq on claims about weapons of mass destruction that proved false; Iraq's long, costly occupation split the country and discredited the neoconservative vision

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the occupation was long and costly and the stated claims proved false.
option_explanations.B: Right because the false claims and the occupation's costs discredited the neoconservative project.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the invasion was framed and justified within the post-9/11 War on Terror.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the claimed weapons were never found; the claims proved false.

options: (A) The invasion achieved its stated goals quickly and retained broad lasting public support
(B) False WMD claims and a costly occupation discredited the neoconservative vision of remaking the region
(C) The invasion had no connection to the September 11 attacks or the broader War on Terror at all
(D) Iraq's government possessed the claimed weapons stockpiles, fully vindicating the decision to invade
items.stem: In 2003 the United States invaded Iraq on claims about weapons of mass destruction that proved false; the long occupation split the country. Which statement best evaluates this episode in its historical context?

stimulus.text: The 2003 invasion of Iraq, launched on WMD claims that proved false, led to a long, costly occupation that divided the country.

items.explanation: Clinton's move is the textbook case of triangulation: after the New Right's 1994 congressional takeover and Reagan-era shift in the terms of debate, a Democratic president adopted smaller-government policies — declaring 'the era of big government is over' — to hold the political center.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Bill Clinton triangulated: a Democrat who declared 'the era of big government is over,' signed welfare reform (1996)

option_explanations.A: Wrong because welfare reform moved policy toward work requirements and time limits, not socialist planning.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because no court ordered the law; it was a political choice.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the law restructured aid rather than ending all federal spending on the poor.
option_explanations.D: Right because the New Right's success pulled even Democratic presidents toward smaller-government policies.

options: (A) The Democratic Party's adoption of socialist economic planning and centralized state control
(B) A Supreme Court order requiring Congress to pass the law
(C) The complete end of all federal spending on the poor
(D) Triangulation: New Right success pulled a Democratic president toward smaller government
items.stem: In 1996, Democratic President Clinton signed welfare reform replacing open-ended federal aid with time-limited, work-conditioned assistance — after declaring 'the era of big government is over.' Which broader development best explains this action by a Democratic president?

stimulus.text: Welfare reform (1996): the law replacing open-ended federal welfare with time-limited, work-conditioned aid, signed by President Clinton.

items.explanation: The Tea Party rose from the populist backlash the review describes: TARP bailouts fed fury on left and right after 2008, and the ACA — the decade's defining political war — gave that anger a concrete target, mobilizing a revolt against federal spending and government expansion.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — the bank bailouts (TARP) saved the system and fed a populist fury on both left and right; the Affordable Care Act became the decade's defining political war, fueling the Tea Party revolt; §What the exam tests here — polarization markers: the Tea Party

option_explanations.A: Right because post-2008 populist anger at bailouts, spending, and the ACA drove the revolt.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the Tea Party opposed the ACA and federal health-care expansion.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the Tea Party was a conservative grassroots movement, not a Democratic establishment project.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the movement's targets were post-2008 spending and the ACA, not 1980s tax cuts.

options: (A) Backlash against bank bailouts, federal spending, and the health-care law after 2008
(B) Support for expanding the federal government's role in health care and social programs
(C) A movement led and funded by the Democratic Party establishment
(D) Opposition to Reagan-era tax cuts and supply-side economics
items.stem: The Tea Party revolt emerged after 2008-2010. Which broader development best explains the context of its rise?

stimulus.text: The Tea Party revolt: a conservative grassroots backlash that grew after the 2008 bank bailouts and the fight over the Affordable Care Act.
